claim: Adolescent synaptic pruning is thought to enable optimal cognition because it is disrupted in certain neuropathologies.
source: Adolescent synaptic pruning is thought to enable optimal cognition because it is disrupted in certain neuropathologies, yet the initiator of this process is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references the relationship between synaptic pruning and cognition based on observations in neuropathologies.

claim: The initiator of adolescent synaptic pruning is unknown.
source: Adolescent synaptic pruning is thought to enable optimal cognition because it is disrupted in certain neuropathologies, yet the initiator of this process is unknown.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: The α4βδ GABAA receptor is an extrasynaptic inhibitory receptor which first emerges on dendritic spines at puberty in female mice.
source: One factor not yet considered is the α4βδ GABAA receptor (GABAR), an extrasynaptic inhibitory receptor which first emerges on dendritic spines at puberty in female mice.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research from the authors as referenced in the introduction.

claim: α4βδ GABARs trigger adolescent pruning.
source: Here we show that α4βδ GABARs trigger adolescent pruning.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells decreased by half post-pubertally in female wild-type mice.
source: Spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells decreased by half post-pubertally in female wild-type but not α4 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells did not decrease post-pubertally in female α4 KO mice.
source: Spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells decreased by half post-pubertally in female wild-type but not α4 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The decrease in spine density at puberty was associated with decreased expression of kalirin-7 (Kal7).
source: This effect was associated with decreased expression of kalirin-7 (Kal7), a spine protein which controls actin cytoskeleton remodeling.
evidence: This association is supported by immunocytochemistry data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Kalirin-7 is a spine protein which controls actin cytoskeleton remodeling.
source: This effect was associated with decreased expression of kalirin-7 (Kal7), a spine protein which controls actin cytoskeleton remodeling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kal7 function, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Kal7 decreased at puberty as a result of reduced NMDAR activation due to α4βδ-mediated inhibition.
source: Kal7 decreased at puberty as a result of reduced NMDAR activation due to α4βδ-mediated inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data showing reduced NMDAR current and immunocytochemistry showing Kal7 expression changes.

claim: In the absence of α4βδ-mediated inhibition, Kal7 expression was unchanged at puberty.
source: In the absence of this inhibition, Kal7 expression was unchanged at puberty.
evidence: This is supported by data from α4 KO mice showing maintained Kal7 expression.

claim: In the unpruned condition, spatial re-learning was impaired.
source: In the unpruned condition, spatial re-learning was impaired.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from α4 KO mice and mice treated with MK-801.

claim: Pubertal pruning requires α4βδ GABARs.
source: These data suggest that pubertal pruning requires α4βδ GABARs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that pruning does not occur in α4 KO mice.

claim: In the absence of α4βδ GABARs, pruning is prevented and cognition is not optimal.
source: In their absence, pruning is prevented and cognition is not optimal.
evidence: This is supported by spine density data and behavioral testing in α4 KO mice.

claim: During the pubertal period, the density of dendritic spines decreases by half in widespread areas of the CNS.
source: During the pubertal period, the density of dendritic spines decreases by half in widespread areas of the CNS (Huttenlocher, 1979; Zehr et al., 2006; Petanjek et al., 2011; Koss et al., 2014), including the CA1 hippocampus and temporal lobe of both rodents (Yildirim et al., 2008) and humans (Tang et al., 2014), sites essential for learning and memory (Pastalkova, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Spine density decreases by half in the CA1 hippocampus and temporal lobe of both rodents and humans during the pubertal period.
source: During the pubertal period, the density of dendritic spines decreases by half in widespread areas of the CNS (Huttenlocher, 1979; Zehr et al., 2006; Petanjek et al., 2011; Koss et al., 2014), including the CA1 hippocampus and temporal lobe of both rodents (Yildirim et al., 2008) and humans (Tang et al., 2014), sites essential for learning and memory (Pastalkova, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in rodents and humans.

claim: CA1 hippocampus and temporal lobe are sites essential for learning and memory.
source: During the pubertal period, the density of dendritic spines decreases by half in widespread areas of the CNS (Huttenlocher, 1979; Zehr et al., 2006; Petanjek et al., 2011; Koss et al., 2014), including the CA1 hippocampus and temporal lobe of both rodents (Yildirim et al., 2008) and humans (Tang et al., 2014), sites essential for learning and memory (Pastalkova, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Dendritic spines express NMDA receptors (NMDARs) at excitatory synapses.
source: Dendritic spines express NMDA receptors (NMDARs) at excitatory synapses (Matsuzaki et al., 2004) which can be activated to form memory traces (Bannerman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NMDARs can be activated to form memory traces.
source: Dendritic spines express NMDA receptors (NMDARs) at excitatory synapses (Matsuzaki et al., 2004) which can be activated to form memory traces (Bannerman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A modelling study suggests that an optimal spine density, produced by developmental pruning of unnecessary synapses, may be necessary for the ability to form memories and to re-learn or 'update' previously learned information.
source: A modelling study (Ruppin, 1999) suggests that an optimal spine density, produced by developmental pruning of unnecessary synapses, may be necessary not only for the ability to form memories but also the ability to re-learn or 'update' previously learned information.
evidence: This claim is based on a cited modeling study.

claim: The mechanisms underlying spine elimination in CA1 hippocampus during puberty are not yet known.
source: Despite the implied importance of synaptic pruning during adolescence, the mechanisms underlying spine elimination in CA1 hippocampus during puberty are not yet known nor are the behavioral outcomes of altered spine density.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The behavioral outcomes of altered spine density are not yet known.
source: Despite the implied importance of synaptic pruning during adolescence, the mechanisms underlying spine elimination in CA1 hippocampus during puberty are not yet known nor are the behavioral outcomes of altered spine density.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Scavenging by immune system components such as the microglia plays a role in spine pruning at certain times in development.
source: At certain times in development, scavenging by immune system components such as the microglia plays a role in spine pruning (Schafer et al., 2012; Sekar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The immune system is likely the final step in synapse elimination in several CNS areas including the CA3 hippocampus.
source: This system is likely the final step in synapse elimination in several CNS areas including the CA3 hippocampus, but does not have a role in synapse loss of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells during puberty (Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on cited research and inference about the role of the immune system.

claim: The immune system does not have a role in synapse loss of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells during puberty.
source: This system is likely the final step in synapse elimination in several CNS areas including the CA3 hippocampus, but does not have a role in synapse loss of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells during puberty (Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: GABARs mediate most inhibition in the brain.
source: GABARs mediate most inhibition in the brain and are pentameric membrane proteins, of diverse sub-type, which conduct a Cl- current.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GABAR function.

claim: GABARs are pentameric membrane proteins, of diverse sub-type, which conduct a Cl- current.
source: GABARs mediate most inhibition in the brain and are pentameric membrane proteins, of diverse sub-type, which conduct a Cl- current.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GABAR structure and function.

claim: In the hippocampus, GABARs are either expressed sub-synaptically, where they generate a phasic current, or extrasynaptically, where they underlie a tonic inhibitory conductance.
source: In the hippocampus, GABARs are either expressed sub-synaptically, where they generate a phasic current, or extrasynaptically, where they underlie a tonic inhibitory conductance (Stell and Mody, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: During the pubertal period (PND 35–44) of female mice, α4βδ GABARs transiently emerge on dendritic spines of CA1 pyramidal cells, adjacent to excitatory synapses.
source: During the pubertal period (PND 35–44) of female mice, we have shown that α4βδ GABARs transiently emerge on dendritic spines of CA1 pyramidal cells, adjacent to excitatory synapses (Shen et al., 2010; Aoki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: α4βδ GABARs are extrasynaptic receptors sensitive to low levels of ambient GABA (<1 μM).
source: These extrasynaptic receptors, which are sensitive to low levels of ambient GABA (<1 μM) (Brown et al., 2002), generate a shunting inhibition which reduces NMDAR-generated current (Shen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: α4βδ GABARs generate a shunting inhibition which reduces NMDAR-generated current.
source: These extrasynaptic receptors, which are sensitive to low levels of ambient GABA (<1 μM) (Brown et al., 2002), generate a shunting inhibition which reduces NMDAR-generated current (Shen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: NMDA current is robust in pubertal mice lacking expression of α4βδ GABARs.
source: However, NMDA current is robust in pubertal mice lacking expression of α4βδ GABARs (Shen et al., 2010), suggesting that the inhibition mediated by α4βδ GABARs produces the impairment rather than a lack of functional NMDARs at puberty.
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The inhibition mediated by α4βδ GABARs produces the impairment in NMDAR current rather than a lack of functional NMDARs at puberty.
source: However, NMDA current is robust in pubertal mice lacking expression of α4βδ GABARs (Shen et al., 2010), suggesting that the inhibition mediated by α4βδ GABARs produces the impairment rather than a lack of functional NMDARs at puberty.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NMDAR current is normal in α4 KO mice.

claim: The pubertal increase in hippocampal α4βδ GABAR expression prevents induction of long-term potentiation.
source: We have also shown that the pubertal increase in hippocampal α4βδ GABAR expression prevents induction of long-term potentiation, an in vitro model of learning, and impairs spatial learning of female mice (Shen et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: The pubertal increase in hippocampal α4βδ GABAR expression impairs spatial learning of female mice.
source: We have also shown that the pubertal increase in hippocampal α4βδ GABAR expression prevents induction of long-term potentiation, an in vitro model of learning, and impairs spatial learning of female mice (Shen et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Learning and memory deficits at puberty were not observed in α4 KO mice.
source: These deficits were not observed at puberty in α4 KO (Shen et al., 2016) or δ KO (Shen et al., 2010) mice, implicating pubertal α4βδ GABARs as the mediating factor.
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Learning and memory deficits at puberty were not observed in δ KO mice.
source: These deficits were not observed at puberty in α4 KO (Shen et al., 2016) or δ KO (Shen et al., 2010) mice, implicating pubertal α4βδ GABARs as the mediating factor.
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Expression of α4βδ GABARs at the onset of puberty initiates synaptic pruning in the female mouse hippocampus.
source: We have extended these studies to show here that expression of α4βδ GABARs at the onset of puberty initiates synaptic pruning in the female mouse hippocampus, which ultimately reduces spine density post-pubertally (comparing spine density at PND 35 versus PND 56).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: In the α4 KO mouse, pruning does not take place.
source: In the α4 KO mouse, pruning does not take place and the cognitive ability of the post-pubertal mice is impaired.
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements in α4 KO mice.

claim: The cognitive ability of post-pubertal α4 KO mice is impaired.
source: In the α4 KO mouse, pruning does not take place and the cognitive ability of the post-pubertal mice is impaired.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data.

claim: α4βδ-triggered pruning is due to impairment of NMDAR activation which regulates expression of kalirin-7 (Kal7).
source: We further suggest that α4βδ-triggered pruning is due to impairment of NMDAR activation which regulates expression of kalirin-7 (Kal7), a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) important for stabilizing the actin cytoskeleton (Penzes et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by data on NMDAR current, Kal7 expression, and spine density.

claim: Kalirin-7 is a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) important for stabilizing the actin cytoskeleton.
source: We further suggest that α4βδ-triggered pruning is due to impairment of NMDAR activation which regulates expression of kalirin-7 (Kal7), a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) important for stabilizing the actin cytoskeleton (Penzes et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Spine density of both proximal and distal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells decreased ~50% from PND 35 to PND 56 in female mice.
source: Spine density of both proximal and distal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells decreased ~50% from PND 35 (puberty onset) to PND 56 (post-pubertal, p<0.05) in female mice (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: There was no significant change in spine density during adolescence in α4 KO mice.
source: In contrast to the wild-type (WT) mice, there was no significant change in spine density during adolescence in α4 KO mice, for which spine density was 100–150% greater than in WT mice post-pubertally (p<0.05), implicating α4βδ GABARs in spine pruning (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Spine density in α4 KO mice was 100–150% greater than in WT mice post-pubertally.
source: In contrast to the wild-type (WT) mice, there was no significant change in spine density during adolescence in α4 KO mice, for which spine density was 100–150% greater than in WT mice post-pubertally (p<0.05), implicating α4βδ GABARs in spine pruning (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Adolescent synaptic pruning was also observed in the male.
source: Adolescent synaptic pruning was also observed in the male (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), where α4βδ GABAR expression is also increased at puberty (unpublished data): Spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells decreased by ~42% from puberty to post-puberty (p<0.05), an effect not observed in the male α4 KO mouse.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: α4βδ GABAR expression is increased at puberty in males.
source: Adolescent synaptic pruning was also observed in the male (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), where α4βδ GABAR expression is also increased at puberty (unpublished data): Spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells decreased by ~42% from puberty to post-puberty (p<0.05), an effect not observed in the male α4 KO mouse.
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data from the authors.

claim: Spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells decreased by ~42% from puberty to post-puberty in male mice.
source: Adolescent synaptic pruning was also observed in the male (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), where α4βδ GABAR expression is also increased at puberty (unpublished data): Spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells decreased by ~42% from puberty to post-puberty (p<0.05), an effect not observed in the male α4 KO mouse.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The decrease in spine density from puberty to post-puberty was not observed in the male α4 KO mouse.
source: Adolescent synaptic pruning was also observed in the male (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), where α4βδ GABAR expression is also increased at puberty (unpublished data): Spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells decreased by ~42% from puberty to post-puberty (p<0.05), an effect not observed in the male α4 KO mouse.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mushroom spines decreased by ~85% post-pubertally in WT mice.
source: Mushroom spines, thought to be 'learning spines' (Bourne and Harris, 2007), decreased by ~85%, while stubby spines decreased by 50% post-pubertally in WT mice (p<0.05); α4 knock-out prevented these changes, resulting in a 500–600% increase in mushroom spines and a 40% decrease in thin spines (p<0.05; Figure 1c,d) compared to the WT post-pubertal hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: Mushroom spines are thought to be 'learning spines'.
source: Mushroom spines, thought to be 'learning spines' (Bourne and Harris, 2007), decreased by ~85%, while stubby spines decreased by 50% post-pubertally in WT mice (p<0.05); α4 knock-out prevented these changes, resulting in a 500–600% increase in mushroom spines and a 40% decrease in thin spines (p<0.05; Figure 1c,d) compared to the WT post-pubertal hippocampus.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Stubby spines decreased by 50% post-pubertally in WT mice.
source: Mushroom spines, thought to be 'learning spines' (Bourne and Harris, 2007), decreased by ~85%, while stubby spines decreased by 50% post-pubertally in WT mice (p<0.05); α4 knock-out prevented these changes, resulting in a 500–600% increase in mushroom spines and a 40% decrease in thin spines (p<0.05; Figure 1c,d) compared to the WT post-pubertal hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: α4 knock-out prevented the post-pubertal changes in mushroom and stubby spines.
source: Mushroom spines, thought to be 'learning spines' (Bourne and Harris, 2007), decreased by ~85%, while stubby spines decreased by 50% post-pubertally in WT mice (p<0.05); α4 knock-out prevented these changes, resulting in a 500–600% increase in mushroom spines and a 40% decrease in thin spines (p<0.05; Figure 1c,d) compared to the WT post-pubertal hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: α4 knock-out resulted in a 500–600% increase in mushroom spines compared to the WT post-pubertal hippocampus.
source: Mushroom spines, thought to be 'learning spines' (Bourne and Harris, 2007), decreased by ~85%, while stubby spines decreased by 50% post-pubertally in WT mice (p<0.05); α4 knock-out prevented these changes, resulting in a 500–600% increase in mushroom spines and a 40% decrease in thin spines (p<0.05; Figure 1c,d) compared to the WT post-pubertal hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: α4 knock-out resulted in a 40% decrease in thin spines compared to the WT post-pubertal hippocampus.
source: Mushroom spines, thought to be 'learning spines' (Bourne and Harris, 2007), decreased by ~85%, while stubby spines decreased by 50% post-pubertally in WT mice (p<0.05); α4 knock-out prevented these changes, resulting in a 500–600% increase in mushroom spines and a 40% decrease in thin spines (p<0.05; Figure 1c,d) compared to the WT post-pubertal hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: Dendritic length was unaltered across pubertal stages and genotypes.
source: Dendritic length was unaltered (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Decreased spine density in WT post-pubertal hippocampus was accompanied by decreased frequency of miniature excitatory post-synaptic currents (mEPSCs).
source: Decreased spine density in WT post-pubertal hippocampus was accompanied by decreased frequency of miniature excitatory post-synaptic currents (mEPSCs), reflecting fewer synapses, compared with the α4 KO hippocampus (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: Decreased mEPSC frequency reflects fewer synapses.
source: Decreased spine density in WT post-pubertal hippocampus was accompanied by decreased frequency of miniature excitatory post-synaptic currents (mEPSCs), reflecting fewer synapses, compared with the α4 KO hippocampus (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between mEPSC frequency and synapse number.

claim: NMDA-generated current was reduced at puberty even after blockade of GABARs at inhibitory synapses with 200 nM SR95531.
source: NMDA-generated current was reduced at puberty (Figure 2a,b), even after blockade of GABARs at inhibitory synapses with 200 nM SR95531 (Stell and Mody, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: 200 nM SR95531 blocks GABARs at inhibitory synapses.
source: NMDA-generated current was reduced at puberty (Figure 2a,b), even after blockade of GABARs at inhibitory synapses with 200 nM SR95531 (Stell and Mody, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NMDAR current was robust in the α4 KO hippocampus.
source: In contrast, NMDAR current was robust in the α4 KO hippocampus (Figure 2a,b), as we have previously shown for the δ KO hippocampus (Shen et al., 2010), and after total GABAR blockade with 120 μM SR95531 (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: NMDAR current was robust in the δ KO hippocampus.
source: In contrast, NMDAR current was robust in the α4 KO hippocampus (Figure 2a,b), as we have previously shown for the δ KO hippocampus (Shen et al., 2010), and after total GABAR blockade with 120 μM SR95531 (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: NMDAR current was robust after total GABAR blockade with 120 μM SR95531.
source: In contrast, NMDAR current was robust in the α4 KO hippocampus (Figure 2a,b), as we have previously shown for the δ KO hippocampus (Shen et al., 2010), and after total GABAR blockade with 120 μM SR95531 (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: MK-801 was administered at a dose shown to increase hippocampal NMDAR expression compensatorily.
source: To this end, MK-801 was administered, at a dose shown to increase hippocampal NMDAR expression compensatorily (Gao and Tamminga, 1995), during the pubertal period (0.25 mg/kg,i.p., once daily for 10 days).
evidence: This is based on cited research showing the effect of MK-801 on NMDAR expression.

claim: Pubertal MK-801 administration increased spine density by 100% in both proximal and distal dendrites post-pubertally.
source: Pubertal MK-801 administration increased spine density by 100% in both proximal and distal dendrites post-pubertally (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements after MK-801 treatment.

claim: Pubertal MK-801 administration reflected a significant increase in the density of mushroom and stubby spines.
source: This reflected a significant increase in the density of mushroom and stubby spines (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 2c-e.

claim: Blockade of NMDARs with memantine, which does not alter NMDAR expression, administered to pubertal α4 KO mice reduced spine density post-pubertally by 50%.
source: Conversely, blockade of NMDARs with memantine, which does not alter NMDAR expression (Cole et al., 2013), administered to pubertal α4 KO mice reduced spine density post-pubertally by 50% (p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements after memantine treatment.

claim: Memantine does not alter NMDAR expression.
source: Conversely, blockade of NMDARs with memantine, which does not alter NMDAR expression (Cole et al., 2013), administered to pubertal α4 KO mice reduced spine density post-pubertally by 50% (p<0.01).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Memantine decreased mushroom and stubby spines and increased thin spines.
source: Memantine decreased mushroom and stubby spines and increased thin spines (p<0.05, Figure 2f–h).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 2f-h.

claim: Reduced NMDAR activity mediates synaptic pruning at puberty.
source: These data suggest that reduced NMDAR activity mediates synaptic pruning at puberty and that α4βδ GABARs are novel regulators of NMDARs which trigger this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on NMDAR manipulation and spine density.

claim: α4βδ GABARs are novel regulators of NMDARs which trigger synaptic pruning.
source: These data suggest that reduced NMDAR activity mediates synaptic pruning at puberty and that α4βδ GABARs are novel regulators of NMDARs which trigger this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the relationship between α4βδ GABARs, NMDAR activity, and spine density.

claim: α5βγ2 is the primary extrasynaptic GABAR in CA1 hippocampus.
source: In contrast to α4βδ GABARs, α5βγ2, the primary extrasynaptic GABAR in CA1 hippocampus (Caraiscos et al., 2004), did not impair NMDAR activation during puberty.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: α5βγ2 GABARs did not impair NMDAR activation during puberty.
source: In contrast to α4βδ GABARs, α5βγ2, the primary extrasynaptic GABAR in CA1 hippocampus (Caraiscos et al., 2004), did not impair NMDAR activation during puberty.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing no effect of α5 GABAR blockade on NMDAR current.

claim: L-655,708 (50 nM) is a partial inverse agonist that reduces current through α5βγ2 GABARs.
source: Reduction of current through α5βγ2 GABARs was accomplished with the partial inverse agonist L-655,708 (L655, 50 nM) (Ramerstorfer et al., 2010), which had no effect on evoked NMDA current (Figure 2a,b) recorded from pubertal slices.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the drug, supported by citation.

claim: L-655,708 (50 nM) had no effect on evoked NMDA current recorded from pubertal slices.
source: Reduction of current through α5βγ2 GABARs was accomplished with the partial inverse agonist L-655,708 (L655, 50 nM) (Ramerstorfer et al., 2010), which had no effect on evoked NMDA current (Figure 2a,b) recorded from pubertal slices.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Pubertal administration of L655 produced no change in spine density post-pubertally.
source: As predicted, pubertal administration of L655 produced no change in spine density post-pubertally (Figure 3), nor did the benzodiazepine lorazepam (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) which targets the primarily synaptic γ2-containing GABARs (Sigel, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by spine density data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The benzodiazepine lorazepam, which targets the primarily synaptic γ2-containing GABARs, produced no change in spine density post-pubertally when administered during puberty.
source: As predicted, pubertal administration of L655 produced no change in spine density post-pubertally (Figure 3), nor did the benzodiazepine lorazepam (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) which targets the primarily synaptic γ2-containing GABARs (Sigel, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by spine density data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lorazepam targets the primarily synaptic γ2-containing GABARs.
source: As predicted, pubertal administration of L655 produced no change in spine density post-pubertally (Figure 3), nor did the benzodiazepine lorazepam (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) which targets the primarily synaptic γ2-containing GABARs (Sigel, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: α4βδ GABARs selectively reduce spine density at puberty.
source: These findings suggest that α4βδ GABARs selectively reduce spine density at puberty.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that blockade of other GABAR subtypes does not affect spine density.

claim: Total GABAR blockade during puberty with picrotoxin prevented pruning post-pubertally.
source: As expected, total GABAR blockade during puberty (picrotoxin, 3 mg/kg, i.p.) prevented pruning post-pubertally (Figure 3), increasing spine density by ~200%.
evidence: This is supported by spine density data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Total GABAR blockade during puberty increased spine density by ~200% post-pubertally.
source: As expected, total GABAR blockade during puberty (picrotoxin, 3 mg/kg, i.p.) prevented pruning post-pubertally (Figure 3), increasing spine density by ~200%.
evidence: This is supported by spine density data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Total GABAR blockade during puberty increased both mushroom (>900%) and stubby (100%) spines while thin spines were decreased (75%).
source: Both mushroom (>900%) and stubby (100%) spines were increased while thin spines were decreased (75%, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data.

claim: Kal7 is necessary for maintenance of spine number.
source: Because Kal7 is necessary for maintenance of spine number (Ma et al., 2003), we tested the hypothesis that synaptic pruning may be mediated by the decrease in Kal7 expression at the onset of puberty.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Kal7 expression in hippocampal dendrites decreased by almost 50% at puberty compared to pre-puberty.
source: Kal7 expression in hippocampal dendrites decreased by almost 50% at puberty (p<0.05) compared to pre-puberty (PND 28–30), an effect prevented by knock-out of α4, which increased its expression by ~120% (p<0.001) (Figure 4a–d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Knock-out of α4 prevented the pubertal decrease in Kal7 expression and increased its expression by ~120%.
source: Kal7 expression in hippocampal dendrites decreased by almost 50% at puberty (p<0.05) compared to pre-puberty (PND 28–30), an effect prevented by knock-out of α4, which increased its expression by ~120% (p<0.001) (Figure 4a–d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Kal7 expression is activity-dependent.
source: We tested whether NMDARs played a role in Kal7 expression, which is activity-dependent (Ma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Increasing NMDAR expression at puberty increased Kal7 expression by ~100%.
source: Increasing NMDAR expression at puberty increased Kal7 expression by ~100% (p<0.001; Figure 4e,f), while NMDAR blockade with memantine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) reduced Kal7 expression by ~50% in the adult CA1 hippocampus (Figure 4g,h).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4e,f.

claim: NMDAR blockade with memantine reduced Kal7 expression by ~50% in the adult CA1 hippocampus.
source: Increasing NMDAR expression at puberty increased Kal7 expression by ~100% (p<0.001; Figure 4e,f), while NMDAR blockade with memantine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) reduced Kal7 expression by ~50% in the adult CA1 hippocampus (Figure 4g,h).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4g,h.

claim: Activity-dependent expression of Kal7 requires NMDAR activation that is regulated by α4βδ-mediated inhibition.
source: These findings suggest that activity-dependent expression of Kal7 requires NMDAR activation that is regulated by α4βδ-mediated inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on NMDAR activity, α4βδ GABARs, and Kal7 expression.

claim: Synaptic pruning was prevented in the Kal7 KO mouse.
source: In fact, synaptic pruning was prevented in the Kal7 KO, for which spine density was reduced by 40% for both age groups (Figure 4i,j).
evidence: This is supported by spine density data from Kal7 KO mice shown in Figure 4i,j.

claim: Spine density in Kal7 KO mice was reduced by 40% for both pubertal and post-pubertal age groups compared to wild-type.
source: In fact, synaptic pruning was prevented in the Kal7 KO, for which spine density was reduced by 40% for both age groups (Figure 4i,j).
evidence: This is supported by spine density data from Kal7 KO mice shown in Figure 4i,j.

claim: Synaptic pruning may require the decrease in Kal7 expression at puberty in the WT mouse.
source: These data suggest that synaptic pruning may require the decrease in Kal7 expression at puberty in the WT mouse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that pruning does not occur in Kal7 KO mice.

claim: Theoretical analysis has suggested that high densities of mature mushroom spines impair changes in synaptic strength.
source: Theoretical analysis has suggested that high densities of mature mushroom spines impair changes in synaptic strength (Ruppin, 1999), thus predicting that long-term depression (LTD) would be impaired by the high density of mature spines in post-pubertal α4 KO hippocampus.
evidence: This is based on a cited modeling study.

claim: Long-term depression (LTD) was impaired in post-pubertal α4 KO hippocampus.
source: This was the case, where an 8 ± 2.1% depression was observed 1 hr after low frequency stimulation (LFS) compared to the 32 ± 8.4% depression observed in post-pubertal WT hippocampus (p<0.05, Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: An 8 ± 2.1% depression was observed 1 hr after low frequency stimulation in post-pubertal α4 KO hippocampus.
source: This was the case, where an 8 ± 2.1% depression was observed 1 hr after low frequency stimulation (LFS) compared to the 32 ± 8.4% depression observed in post-pubertal WT hippocampus (p<0.05, Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A 32 ± 8.4% depression was observed 1 hr after low frequency stimulation in post-pubertal WT hippocampus.
source: This was the case, where an 8 ± 2.1% depression was observed 1 hr after low frequency stimulation (LFS) compared to the 32 ± 8.4% depression observed in post-pubertal WT hippocampus (p<0.05, Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Theta burst-induction of NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP) was not altered in α4 KO post-pubertal hippocampus.
source: In contrast, theta burst-induction of NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP), an in vitro model of learning, was not altered in α4 KO post-pubertal hippocampus (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Post-pubertal α4 KO mice showed impaired acquisition and retention of the second location in the active place avoidance task.
source: In both tasks, post-pubertal α4 KO mice showed impaired acquisition and retention of the second location, despite initial learning scores similar to WT mice (Figure 5c-d, f).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5c-d.

claim: Post-pubertal α4 KO mice showed impaired acquisition and retention of the second location in the multiple placement object relocation task.
source: In both tasks, post-pubertal α4 KO mice showed impaired acquisition and retention of the second location, despite initial learning scores similar to WT mice (Figure 5c-d, f).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Initial learning scores were similar between post-pubertal α4 KO and WT mice.
source: In both tasks, post-pubertal α4 KO mice showed impaired acquisition and retention of the second location, despite initial learning scores similar to WT mice (Figure 5c-d, f).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5c-d, f.

claim: The impairment in re-learning in α4 KO mice was a cognitive deficit because locomotor activity, shock tolerance and object interest did not differ from WT.
source: This was a cognitive deficit because locomotor activity, shock tolerance and object interest did not differ from WT (Figure 5e,g).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral control data shown in Figure 5e,g.

claim: Reducing synaptic pruning in the WT mouse with MK-801 impaired re-learning performance on MPORT.
source: As predicted, reducing synaptic pruning in the WT mouse with MK-801 impaired re-learning performance on MPORT, while restoring synaptic pruning in the α4 KO mice by blocking NMDARs with memantine, improved performance on this task (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Restoring synaptic pruning in the α4 KO mice by blocking NMDARs with memantine improved re-learning performance on MPORT.
source: As predicted, reducing synaptic pruning in the WT mouse with MK-801 impaired re-learning performance on MPORT, while restoring synaptic pruning in the α4 KO mice by blocking NMDARs with memantine, improved performance on this task (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optimal cognition in adulthood is dependent upon adequate synaptic pruning in adolescence.
source: These data suggest that optimal cognition in adulthood is dependent upon adequate synaptic pruning in adolescence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing impaired re-learning in unpruned conditions.

claim: Initial learning resulted in a ~150% increase in mushroom spine-types.
source: Initial learning resulted in a ~150% increase in mushroom spine-types (p<0.05), with similar increases in stubby spine types (~200%, p<0.05) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Initial learning resulted in similar increases in stubby spine types (~200%).
source: Initial learning resulted in a ~150% increase in mushroom spine-types (p<0.05), with similar increases in stubby spine types (~200%, p<0.05) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 6.

claim: After the second learning trial (re-learning), mushroom spine types were additionally increased by ~50–100%.
source: After the second learning trial (re-learning), mushroom spine types were additionally increased by ~50–100% (p<0.05), while thin spine types were decreased by ~70% (Figure 6); the density of stubby spines did not change significantly.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 6.

claim: After re-learning, thin spine types were decreased by ~70%.
source: After the second learning trial (re-learning), mushroom spine types were additionally increased by ~50–100% (p<0.05), while thin spine types were decreased by ~70% (Figure 6); the density of stubby spines did not change significantly.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The density of stubby spines did not change significantly after re-learning.
source: After the second learning trial (re-learning), mushroom spine types were additionally increased by ~50–100% (p<0.05), while thin spine types were decreased by ~70% (Figure 6); the density of stubby spines did not change significantly.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Increases in mushroom spine density accompanied both learning and re-learning trials.
source: Thus, increases in mushroom spine density accompanied both learning and re-learning trials.
evidence: This is a summary of the spine morphology data from learning experiments.

claim: Pubertal administration of picrotoxin to block GABARs prevented synaptic pruning and impaired re-learning in the post-pubertal mouse.
source: Pubertal administration of picrotoxin (3 mg/kg, i.p.) to block GABARs also prevented synaptic pruning (Figure 3) and impaired re-learning (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) in the post-pubertal mouse.
evidence: This is supported by spine density and behavioral data.

claim: After picrotoxin treatment, mushroom spine density was almost 300% greater in the naïve condition compared to the untreated mouse.
source: Under these conditions, mushroom spine density was almost 300% greater in the naïve condition compared to the untreated mouse (Figure 3, 6), and additional increases in mushroom spine density were only observed after learning (~50% increase, p<0.05), but not after relearning (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: After picrotoxin treatment, additional increases in mushroom spine density were only observed after learning (~50% increase), but not after relearning.
source: Under these conditions, mushroom spine density was almost 300% greater in the naïve condition compared to the untreated mouse (Figure 3, 6), and additional increases in mushroom spine density were only observed after learning (~50% increase, p<0.05), but not after relearning (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Only successful learning/re-learning increases the mushroom spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: Because re-learning was impaired in this unpruned condition, these findings suggest that only successful learning/re-learning increases the mushroom spine density of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that mushroom spines did not increase after unsuccessful re-learning in picrotoxin-treated mice.

claim: Pubertal synaptic pruning is seen in many CNS areas.
source: Pubertal synaptic pruning is seen in many CNS areas (Huttenlocher, 1979; Zehr et al., 2006; Petanjek et al., 2011), and is correlated with EEG changes in humans (Campbell et al., 2012), where the steepest reduction in slow wave (delta, 1–4 Hz) activity occurs at the onset of puberty.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pubertal synaptic pruning is correlated with EEG changes in humans.
source: Pubertal synaptic pruning is seen in many CNS areas (Huttenlocher, 1979; Zehr et al., 2006; Petanjek et al., 2011), and is correlated with EEG changes in humans (Campbell et al., 2012), where the steepest reduction in slow wave (delta, 1–4 Hz) activity occurs at the onset of puberty.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The steepest reduction in slow wave (delta, 1–4 Hz) activity occurs at the onset of puberty in humans.
source: Pubertal synaptic pruning is seen in many CNS areas (Huttenlocher, 1979; Zehr et al., 2006; Petanjek et al., 2011), and is correlated with EEG changes in humans (Campbell et al., 2012), where the steepest reduction in slow wave (delta, 1–4 Hz) activity occurs at the onset of puberty.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: α4βδ GABARs play a critical role in pubertal synaptic pruning.
source: Our findings suggest that α4βδ GABARs play a critical role in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: α4βδ GABARs are uniquely localized to spines during puberty where they reduce NMDAR current.
source: α4βδ GABARs are uniquely localized to spines during puberty where they reduce NMDAR current (Shen et al., 2010), necessary for spine stability (Alvarez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors and others, supported by citations.

claim: NMDAR current is necessary for spine stability.
source: α4βδ GABARs are uniquely localized to spines during puberty where they reduce NMDAR current (Shen et al., 2010), necessary for spine stability (Alvarez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Blockade of the predominant extrasynaptic GABAR in CA1 hippocampus, α5β3γ2, did not facilitate NMDAR activation or alter synaptic pruning during the pubertal period.
source: In contrast, blockade of the predominant extrasynaptic GABAR in CA1 hippocampus, α5β3γ2, did not facilitate NMDAR activation or alter synaptic pruning during the pubertal period, nor did modulation of synaptic γ2-containing GABARs with 200 nM SR95531 or lorazepam.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on NMDAR current and spine density after α5 GABAR blockade.

claim: Modulation of synaptic γ2-containing GABARs with 200 nM SR95531 or lorazepam did not facilitate NMDAR activation or alter synaptic pruning during the pubertal period.
source: In contrast, blockade of the predominant extrasynaptic GABAR in CA1 hippocampus, α5β3γ2, did not facilitate NMDAR activation or alter synaptic pruning during the pubertal period, nor did modulation of synaptic γ2-containing GABARs with 200 nM SR95531 or lorazepam.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on NMDAR current and spine density after synaptic GABAR modulation.

claim: α4βδ GABARs selectively trigger synaptic pruning at puberty via impairment of NMDAR activation.
source: Thus, these findings suggest that α4βδ GABARs selectively trigger synaptic pruning at puberty via impairment of NMDAR activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the specificity of α4βδ GABARs in affecting pruning.

claim: In visual cortex, synaptic α1β2γ2 GABARs target dendritic spines and play a role in spine maturation.
source: This is in contrast to visual cortex, where synaptic α1β2γ2 GABARs target dendritic spines (Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997), and play a role in spine maturation (Heinen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pubertal synaptic pruning is not dependent upon the ovarian hormone estradiol.
source: Pubertal synaptic pruning is not dependent upon the ovarian hormone estradiol (Yildirim et al., 2008), which in fact increases spine density (Woolley et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Estradiol increases spine density.
source: Pubertal synaptic pruning is not dependent upon the ovarian hormone estradiol (Yildirim et al., 2008), which in fact increases spine density (Woolley et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MK-801 administration during the pubertal period of female mice increased the density of dendritic spines post-pubertally, resulting in increases in both mushroom and stubby spine-types.
source: In the present study, MK-801 administration during the pubertal period of female mice increased the density of dendritic spines post-pubertally, resulting in increases in both mushroom and stubby spine-types.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: A recent study reports that similar MK-801 treatment across the peri-pubertal period in male rats also increases the density of stubby spines in hippocampus, but decreases the mushroom spine-types.
source: A recent study (Han et al., 2013) reports that similar MK-801 treatment across the peri-pubertal period in male rats also increases the density of stubby spines in hippocampus, but decreases the mushroom spine-types.
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: MK-801 increases NMDAR expression as a compensatory effect 24 hr after administration (0.1–1.0 mg/kg), selectively in the CA1 region of the hippocampus.
source: Although MK-801 is an NMDA antagonist, it has been shown to increase NMDAR expression, as a compensatory effect 24 hr after administration (0.1–1.0 mg/kg), selectively in the CA1 region of the hippocampus (Gao and Tamminga, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the pre-frontal cortex, only a single low dose of MK-801 increases NMDAR expression on pyramidal cells.
source: In the pre-frontal cortex, only a single low dose of MK-801 increases NMDAR expression on pyramidal cells (Xi et al., 2009), while higher doses have no effect, but decrease NMDAR expression and AMPA receptor-mediated currents of fast-spiking interneurons (Wang and Gao, 2012) suggesting that effects of this drug are cell-type and region specific.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Effects of MK-801 are cell-type and region specific.
source: In the pre-frontal cortex, only a single low dose of MK-801 increases NMDAR expression on pyramidal cells (Xi et al., 2009), while higher doses have no effect, but decrease NMDAR expression and AMPA receptor-mediated currents of fast-spiking interneurons (Wang and Gao, 2012) suggesting that effects of this drug are cell-type and region specific.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research showing differential effects of MK-801 in different cell types and regions.

claim: Other studies have suggested that peri-adolescent administration of MK-801 alters GABAergic circuits in adulthood.
source: Other studies have suggested that peri-adolescent administration of MK-801 alters GABAergic circuits in adulthood (Thomases et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Kal7 binds to the post-synaptic density (PSD).
source: α4βδ GABAR-induced impairment of NMDAR activation at puberty reduces expression of Kal7, a spine protein involved in spine restructuring which binds to the post-synaptic density (PSD) (Penzes et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Kal7 activates the small GTPase Rac1 which regulates the actin cytoskeleton via P21-activated kinases within the spine.
source: Kal7 activates the small GTPase Rac1 which regulates the actin cytoskeleton via P21-activated kinases within the spine (Ma et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Kal7 is one of the few spine proteins shown to be necessary for maintenance of existing spines.
source: Although many proteins localize to the spine, Kal7 is one of the few shown to be necessary for maintenance of existing spines (Penzes et al., 2001; Ma et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A 50% reduction in Kal7 expression at puberty resulted in a 50% decrease in spine number.
source: That may explain results from the present study where a 50% reduction in Kal7 expression at puberty resulted in a 50% decrease in spine number.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Kal7 expression and spine density.

claim: The fact that synaptic pruning was prevented in the absence of Kal7 expression suggests that dynamic regulation of Kal7 expression during adolescence may be one factor underlying synaptic pruning.
source: The fact that synaptic pruning was prevented in the absence of Kal7 expression suggests that dynamic regulation of Kal7 expression during adolescence may be one factor underlying synaptic pruning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that pruning does not occur in Kal7 KO mice.

claim: Many other spine proteins have been identified which alter spine density, including shank3, IQGAP1, valosin, axin and NEDD9.
source: However, many other spine proteins have been identified which alter spine density, including shank3, IQGAP1, valosin, axin and NEDD9 (Roussignol et al., 2005; Gao et al., 2011; Wiesmann et al., 1975; Knutson et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Synaptic remodeling during adolescence may incorporate a more complex array of spine protein changes.
source: Thus, synaptic remodeling during adolescence may incorporate a more complex array of spine protein changes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the knowledge that multiple spine proteins affect spine density.

claim: Several studies have suggested that scavenging by microglia or direct autophagy prunes spines.
source: Several studies have suggested that scavenging by microglia (Schafer et al., 2012) or direct autophagy (Tang et al., 2014) prunes spines.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The C4 complement system is abnormal in schizophrenia.
source: In particular, the C4 complement system is abnormal in schizophrenia; C4 activates C3, which binds to target spines and promotes their engulfment by phagocytic cells (Sekar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: C4 activates C3, which binds to target spines and promotes their engulfment by phagocytic cells.
source: In particular, the C4 complement system is abnormal in schizophrenia; C4 activates C3, which binds to target spines and promotes their engulfment by phagocytic cells (Sekar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The complement system may be target and developmentally specific – as it does not underlie adolescent pruning in CA1 hippocampus.
source: This system may be target and developmentally specific – as it does not underlie adolescent pruning in CA1 hippocampus (Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The involvement of the complement cascade in synaptic pruning would likely be the final step in spine removal and does not preclude involvement of other systems, such as NMDAR inhibition by α4βδ receptors which would be the initial trigger for the pruning process.
source: In addition, the involvement of the complement cascade in synaptic pruning would likely be the final step in spine removal and does not preclude involvement of other systems, such as NMDAR inhibition by α4βδ receptors which would be the initial trigger for the pruning process.
evidence: This is a speculation about the relationship between different mechanisms of synaptic pruning.

claim: The mushroom spines were selectively removed during pubertal synaptic pruning in the wild-type mouse, leaving an abundance of thin spines.
source: The mushroom spines were selectively removed during pubertal synaptic pruning in the wild-type mouse, leaving an abundance of thin spines.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data from the study.

claim: Learning increased mushroom spines.
source: Our results suggest that learning increased mushroom spines, consistent with earlier reports (Beltrán-Campos et al., 2011; González-Ramírez et al., 2014), which we also observed by 2 hr after re-learning, when the density of thin spines also decreased.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology data from learning experiments and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Thin spines express abundant numbers of NMDARs, are highly motile and plastic.
source: These two spine types are well-characterized and sub-serve different functions: Thin spines express abundant numbers of NMDARs, are highly motile and plastic (Kasai et al., 2003; Holtmaat et al., 2006), while the larger mushroom spines are relatively more stable and express AMPA receptors predominantly (Dumitriu et al., 2010; Matsuzaki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The larger mushroom spines are relatively more stable and express AMPA receptors predominantly.
source: These two spine types are well-characterized and sub-serve different functions: Thin spines express abundant numbers of NMDARs, are highly motile and plastic (Kasai et al., 2003; Holtmaat et al., 2006), while the larger mushroom spines are relatively more stable and express AMPA receptors predominantly (Dumitriu et al., 2010; Matsuzaki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Recent studies using two photon technology have shown that smaller 'thin' spines develop enlarged heads and resemble 'mushroom' spines following LTP induction, accompanied by increased expression of AMPA receptors.
source: Recent studies using two photon technology to assess changes in spines produced by NMDAR-dependent LTP, an in vitro model of learning, have shown that smaller 'thin' spines develop enlarged heads and resemble 'mushroom' spines following LTP induction, accompanied by increased expression of AMPA receptors (Hill and Zito, 2013; Kopec et al., 2006; Harvey and Svoboda, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Larger spine heads have larger post-synaptic densities and active zones, consistent with stronger synaptic connections.
source: These larger spine heads have larger post-synaptic densities and active zones, consistent with stronger synaptic connections (Bell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Changes in spine morphology after LTP induction are first observed within 15 min. with peak effects 40 min to 2 hr after LTP induction.
source: Typically, these changes are first observed within 15 min. with peak effects 40 min to 2 hr after LTP induction, similar to the time-course of our effects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the time course of spine changes after LTP.

claim: A high spine density produces cognitive impairment.
source: Our findings suggest that a high spine density produces cognitive impairment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data in unpruned conditions.

claim: Most experimental studies to date have only examined the effect of spine loss on cognition.
source: Although modelling studies have predicted the cognitive outcome of increases in spine density (Ruppin, 1999), most experimental studies to date have only examined the effect of spine loss on cognition (Oaks et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The high spine density in the unpruned condition selectively impaired re-learning, while learning a spatial task was similar to controls.
source: The high spine density in the unpruned condition in the present study selectively impaired re-learning, while learning a spatial task was similar to controls.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the study.

claim: The impairments in re-learning in the unpruned conditions may be due to the higher prevalence of mushroom-type spines and lower density of thin spine-types.
source: The impairments in re-learning in the unpruned conditions may be due to the higher prevalence of mushroom-type spines and lower density of thin spine-types.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the re-learning impairment.

claim: There may be a maximum number of mushroom spines that can be supported by a dendritic segment due to the energy requirement necessary for spine maintenance or due to spatial constraints.
source: There may be a maximum number of mushroom spines that can be supported by a dendritic segment due to the energy requirement necessary for spine maintenance or due to spatial constraints.
evidence: This is a speculation about the limits of spine density.

claim: The lower density of thin spines may have been insufficient to permit successful re-learning.
source: Alternatively, the lower density of thin spines may have been insufficient to permit successful re-learning.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the re-learning impairment.

claim: The changes in spine density observed after learning and re-learning protocols were of the same magnitude as those observed during adolescence, reflecting the high plasticity of spines.
source: The changes in spine density observed after learning and re-learning protocols were of the same magnitude as those observed during adolescence, reflecting the high plasticity of spines, although changes occurred in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is a comparison of the magnitude of spine density changes across different conditions.

claim: Changes in spine types were distinct for adolescence versus learning/re-learning: during learning and re-learning, mushroom spine-types increased, while these spine-types decreased during adolescence.
source: Changes in spine types were distinct for the two events as well: during learning and re-learning, mushroom spine-types increased, while these spine-types decreased during adolescence.
evidence: This is a comparison of spine morphology changes across different conditions.

claim: The spine density of the control, post-pubertal mice may reflect the lower limit of synapse number because these mice were housed in non-enriched cages with limited sensory stimuli.
source: In addition, the spine density of the control, post-pubertal mice may reflect the lower limit of synapse number because these mice were housed in non-enriched cages with limited sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculation about the baseline spine density in the study.

claim: Exposure to more complex environments, even for 1 hr per day, increases spine density in many areas of the CNS, including CA1 hipppocampus.
source: Numerous studies have shown that exposure to more complex environments, even for 1 hr per day, increases spine density in many areas of the CNS, including CA1 hipppocampus (Turner and Greenough, 1985; Jung and Herms, 2014; Kitanishi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Environmental enrichment increases large spines and enhances spine turnover.
source: Recent studies report that environmental enrichment increases large spines and enhances spine turnover (Jung and Herms, 2014; Kitanishi et al., 2009), suggesting that spine dynamics are environmentally specific.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Spine dynamics are environmentally specific.
source: Recent studies report that environmental enrichment increases large spines and enhances spine turnover (Jung and Herms, 2014; Kitanishi et al., 2009), suggesting that spine dynamics are environmentally specific.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research showing effects of environmental enrichment on spines.

claim: LTD induction was impaired in the unpruned condition (α4 KO), consistent with other reports which describe impairment in LTD under conditions where thin spine number is reduced.
source: LTD induction was also impaired in the unpruned condition (α4 KO), consistent with other reports which describe impairment in LTD under conditions where thin spine number is reduced (Spiga et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Two photon studies have shown that LTD induction reduces thin spine number.
source: Two photon studies have indeed shown that this protocol reduces thin spine number (Nägerl et al., 2004), thus suggesting that a critical number of thin spines may be necessary for LTD induction.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A critical number of thin spines may be necessary for LTD induction.
source: Two photon studies have indeed shown that this protocol reduces thin spine number (Nägerl et al., 2004), thus suggesting that a critical number of thin spines may be necessary for LTD induction.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research and the observation that LTD is impaired when thin spines are reduced.

claim: LTD has been suggested as a cellular mechanism underlying synaptic changes necessary for re-learning.
source: LTD has been suggested as a cellular mechanism underlying synaptic changes necessary for re-learning (Nicholls et al., 2008), where weaker synaptic connections mediated by thin spines are reduced.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Studies reporting more massive decreases in thin spine number, as a result of aging or chronic alcohol exposure, also observed impairments in learning and LTP.
source: In contrast to the present results, studies reporting more massive decreases in thin spine number, as a result of aging or chronic alcohol exposure, also observed impairments in learning and LTP (Dumitriu et al., 2010; Spiga et al., 2014), suggesting that the critical number of thin spines necessary for learning is below that required for relearning.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The critical number of thin spines necessary for learning is below that required for relearning.
source: In contrast to the present results, studies reporting more massive decreases in thin spine number, as a result of aging or chronic alcohol exposure, also observed impairments in learning and LTP (Dumitriu et al., 2010; Spiga et al., 2014), suggesting that the critical number of thin spines necessary for learning is below that required for relearning.
